summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web tool that shows, for any landing site and date on the Moon, where the Sun and Earth sit above the local horizon and how long sunlight and direct Earth contact will last.
A lander needs the Sun for power and a clear line to Earth for radio. At the lunar south pole both hover at the horizon, so a nearby ridge or a three-week delay can decide whether a mission works. Existing tools are accurate but slow to compare options with.
Our tool lets users pick a site and date and read the answer in plain words, backed by the numbers. It draws the sky from the site with the real terrain skyline, ranks named sites, scores the whole south polar region on a map, finds the best landing dates, and shows what a schedule slip costs. A 3D Moon and landscape view make the terrain visible.
Sun and Earth positions come from NASA SPICE data and are checked against JPL Horizons; terrain comes from LOLA elevation data.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web tool for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. Pick a site from our list of 20 past and planned missions, type coordinates, or click a point on a 3D Moon, then pick a date. The tool shows where the Sun and Earth sit above the local horizon, whether the lander has sunlight and a direct Earth link, and how long until each is lost.
How it works: We precompute Sun and Earth positions from NASA SPICE data and terrain skylines from LOLA elevation data. The browser turns these into azimuth and elevation, so the site needs no server.
Benefits and impact: Mission teams can answer "what if we slip three weeks or move a few kilometres?" in seconds. The tool ranks named sites, scores the whole south polar region on a map, finds the best landing dates and shows what a delay costs. A plain-language summary and a guided tour make it usable for students and the public.
Creativity: The sky is drawn as the lander would see it, with the real skyline. A 3D landscape shows the terrain around each site in height colours or true sunlight. Our polar map, given no hints, picks out Malapert Massif and Mons Mouton, both Artemis III candidate regions.
What we considered: Accuracy first. Our positions are tested against 1,060 JPL Horizons values, with a largest difference of 0.0001°. We also state limits openly: the tool covers lighting and communication, not landing safety.
Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js and Tailwind CSS for the site; Python, NumPy and SpiceyPy for the data; GitHub Pages for hosting. We used AI coding assistants throughout.
